- Hue, value (lightness), and chroma

- Tristimulus values ( X , Y , Z ) based on CMFs

- International standard, formalizing Munsell's principles
- Lightness ( L *), chroma ( C *), and hue angle ( h )
- Perceptually uniform

## Chromaticity Gamut vs Color Gamut



- RGB triangle areas are often called 'color gamut'
- However, xy and u′v′ areas are not proportional
- u′v′ space is nominally more uniform than xy space
- MacAdam ellipses (MacAdam, JOSA, 1942)
- Sparsely sampled at 10 × JND scale from one observer

- Neither xy nor u′v′ is uniform
- Chromaticity diagrams lack a luminance or lightness axis, limiting their ability to fully represent perceptual color differences

- The color gamut of a display is described as a 3D range in the D50 CIELAB space (SID/ICDM, CIE, IEC)

The historical development of CIE color spaces began with the 1931 CIE Basic Colorimetry, which defined tristimulus values (X, Y, Z) based on CMFs and introduced the (x, y) chromaticity diagram. This system was constructed for practical color reproduction but notably lacked perceptual uniformity. Progressing towards better perceptual representation, the 1976 CIE (L*, a*, b*) system, also known as CIELAB, was established as an international standard. It formalized Munsell's principles by defining lightness (L*), chroma (C*), and hue angle (h), and was designed to be perceptually uniform, though its initial chromatic adaptation transform (CAT) worked only when adapted to a white close to D65. 

In modern color management, the color gamut of a display is described as a 3D range in the D50 CIELAB space, where the original CAT is replaced with the Bradford CAT. D50 CIELAB is also used in ICC profiles as a standard PCS for device-independent color conversion. The Gamut Rings Color Scope, which provides a unified view of lightness, chroma, and hue angle in a perceptually uniform 2D layout, utilizes D65 CIELAB as its reference space, anchored to the input signal's white. The generation of D65 Gamut Rings for color scope involves computing the gamut boundary at constant lightness levels in the D65 CIELAB space, requiring conversion from CIE 1931 (Y, x, y) to CIELAB coordinates. Gamut Rings themselves were standardized in CIE 246:2021 Colour Gamuts for Output Media. While CIELAB (with Bradford CAT) is widely adopted, it still has limitations such as non-uniformity and artifacts in certain regions. Ongoing CIE work on perceptual spaces includes alternatives like CIECAM16 (CIE 248:2022), though it is important to note that CIE standard color spaces and ICtCp employ different chromatic adaptation models and therefore cannot be directly compared.

## Introduction

Since 2015, Trinity College Dublin has offered a Master's-level 'Motion Picture Engineering' (MPE) course within the School of Engineering, uniquely combining core principles of video compositing and streaming with cutting-edge developments in the field. The curriculum includes advanced topics such as motion estimation and compensation, alpha matting, transcoding pipelines, compression and color standards, while also introducing the disruptive role of neural networks in modern post-production workflows. To bridge theory and practice, students gain hands-on experience with Foundry's Nuke software 2 and benefit from guest lectures by professionals from YouTube, Sky, Netflix, Meta, VideoLAN and other industry leaders.

The MPE module consistently attracts students with highly diverse technical backgrounds, creating significant pedagogical challenges. The cohort typically ranges from experienced deep learning practitioners who may lack domain-specific knowledge in traditional image processing techniques, to newcomers who are entirely unfamiliar with both machine learning concepts and digital signal processing fundamentals. This heterogeneous mix of prior knowledge and technical experience necessitates an adaptive teaching approach that simultaneously supports advanced learners while providing foundational support to those beginning their MPE journey.

Recognizing the transformative potential of AI Large Language Models (LLMs) in addressing these challenges and inspired by previous research on LLMs in education [1-5], we identified Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) as a promising technique for developing an AI Teaching Assistant (AI-TA) capable of providing such targeted, course-aware support to students. RAG combines an LLM with external knowledge retrieval to ground responses in domain-specific content, while also reducing hallucinations [6].

While RAG has been applied successfully across numerous domains [5, 7], and represents a well-established paradigm, the practical implementation constraints and classroom integration challenges that emerge during real-world educational deployment remain underexplored. Moving beyond theoretical RAG discussions, this paper addresses the specific technical decisions, operational limitations, and workflow considerations that educators and other professionals must navigate when implementing AI-powered support systems in dynamic, technically complex fields like MPE.

During Spring 2025, we conducted a comprehensive 7-week pilot deployment with all 43 enrolled MPE students, systematically collecting usage data and student feedback to examine both technical performance and human factors influencing AI adoption in a real classroom environment. This case study reveals the practical realities of AI-TA deployment, illuminating the "muddy waters" that AI-TA implementers must navigate - from competing with established tools like ChatGPT 3 , to questioning the benefit of user anonymity, managing an operationally intensive administrator's workflow, and optimizing costs. While the course content was MPEspecific, this case study is applicable across technical education domains. We present our technical implementation approach, key findings, and recommendations for those considering similar deployments. Our code is available on GitHub 1 .

## AI-TA Development

As a well-established architectural pattern, numerous off-the-shelf RAG solutions are available (e.g. Claude Projects 4 , Agenthost 5 ). Our university setting, however necessitated prioritizing ethics, data protection, security and compliance as core requirements, which significantly limited our options. Working within implementation timelines while meeting these requirements, our solution needed to:

- Utilize university-approved technologies and infrastructure
- Enable students to log in and converse with it anonymously
- Provide AI safeguards preventing exposure to harmful or unsuitable content
- Protect conversational data in case of accidental disclosure of personally identifiable or private information
- Comply with local regulations such as the European Union's General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) 6
- Be deployed securely without compromising university network security

Given these constraints, a custom-built AI-TA incorporating services from Microsoft Azure 7 and Azure AI Foundry 8 emerged as the most viable solution, for the following reasons:

- As the university's designated enterprise cloud platform, Azure met approval requirements
- AI Foundry offers specialized tools for building custom RAG-based solutions
- Microsoft provides specially licensed, Azure-hosted copies of OpenAI's latest AI models, which can be configured with content safety filters
- Azure's customer agreement guarantees that customers' data won't be used to further train its AI models
- Customers can choose the geographical locations of their model deployments, data processing and storage, making it easier to comply with regulations like the GDPR
- Azure enables a secure and scalable deployment
- With a custom-built solution, we could implement domain-specific features driven by student feedback, rather than being constrained by commercial product roadmaps

## Architecture & Student Workflow

Given the rapid development of AI technologies, we chose a modular architecture for our AI-TA, simplifying its maintainability. Figure 1 illustrates this architecture at a very high level, as well as a student's workflow to use it, once logged in anonymously.

Figure 1. High-level architecture and student workflow of our AI-TA. An Azure Prompt Flow deployment provides RAG as a service. A custom web application powers the UI, consumes the RAG service and uses an Azure SQL Database to store students' anonymous session data.


Azure Prompt Flow is an Azure-specific abstraction that simplifies the development, iteration and deployment of custom multi-step AI solutions, such as RAG. Using AI Foundry's UI, we designed, configured and deployed our RAG Prompt Flow as a RESTful service on an Azure Virtual Machine, exposing a secure endpoint for application integration. We also developed a custom Python web application leveraging FastAPI 9 to securely and efficiently consume this endpoint, power the AI-TA's conversational UI and manage students' anonymous session data. We deployed the application as a public Azure Web App with anonymous private login and secure connection to a private Azure SQL Database for data storage. Once fully deployed, the student's workflow to use the AI-TA is described in Table 1.

Table 1. Student's step-by-step workflow to use the AI-TA

|   Step | Student's Action                                                                                   | AI-TA's Action                                                                                                                                                           |
|--------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
|      1 | Go to the AI-TA online and log in with anonymous login credentials                                 | Start a new anonymous session and save session details to the database                                                                                                   |
|      2 | Query the AI-TA via its conversational UI, and wait a few seconds for its response                 | Save the query in the database and then forward it to the Prompt Flow endpoint. Save the response in the database, then apply custom formatting and display it on the UI |
|      3 | Continue with the conversation. The AI-TA remembers past queries and responses (i.e. chat history) | Send chat history to the Prompt Flow endpoint along with each query (up to 10 of the most recent query-response exchanges from the current session)                      |
|      4 | Once satisfied, abandon the conversation and/or log out of the AI-TA                               | If the user logged out, close the session immediately. If not, close it after a defined period of chat inactivity (e.g. 12 hours) via regularly scheduled job.           |

## Azure Prompt Flow

Figure 2 takes a deeper look at the computational steps of our custom Azure Prompt Flow, which implements RAG using an Azure AI Search Index of the course materials as a knowledge base along with Azure Open AI's gpt-4o-mini LLM.

Figure 2. Computational steps of our custom RAG Prompt Flow, which uses an Azure AI Search Index of the course materials as a knowledge base and Azure Open AI's gpt-4o-mini LLM.


The Prompt Flow's endpoint accepts two inputs: the student's query, and their recent chat history with the AI-TA, if applicable. Once input(s) are received, it executes the following steps:

1. Pre-Processing: This step screens the query for words and phrases that falsely trigger the AI models' content-safety filters and rephrases them. For example, we found that the phrase 'How do I install Nuke?' had this effect, so it is rephrased as 'How do I install the software Nuke'. It also captures the date and time for use in a downstream step.
2. Retrieve Context: The query is sent to Azure AI Search, which transforms it into a vector embedding plus set of keywords. This dual format enables 'hybrid' comparison against an AI Search Index containing content from the course materials. We used Azure OpenAI's text-embedding-ada-002 model for vectorization with cosine similarity and the K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) algorithm for vector-based retrieval. We tuned key search parameters via manual testing with real course materials prior to launch, settling on K=10 and enabling AI Search's semantic re-ranking capability for a satisfactory balance between retrieval recall and precision 10 .
3. Format Context: This step transforms the raw results from context retrieval to a format suitable for inclusion in an LLM prompt downstream. This format includes not only the

10 At the time of implementation, AI Foundry's UI did not enable custom configuration of keyword extraction and comparison, fusion of vector and keyword search results, or semantic re-ranking

- content of each search result, but also the full-path filename of the document and page on which the content is located. This metadata is needed later for including page-level source citations in the AI-TA's responses, which is a feature we hypothesized students would find useful.
4.  Prompt LLM: In the final step, multiple variables - the date and time, context, query and chat history - are fed to a detailed Prompt Template, and the resulting prompt is forwarded to the LLM ( gpt-4o-mini ). Finally, the LLM's response is output by the Prompt Flow's endpoint.

## Prompt Engineering

The Prompt Template required substantial development effort, with extensive iterations during our pre-launch testing phase. Our final prompt was over 1,800 words, and included specific instructions for:

- Interaction guidelines (examples):
- o 'If a student struggles with a concept, guide them step-by-step instead of just stating the answer.'
- o 'Encourage students to think critically and ask further questions.'
- Scope boundaries (example):
- o 'For broader and/or semi-related questions: Include related general knowledge in your answer, but prioritize information from the context.'
- Date and time awareness for queries about course events such as exam dates (example):
- o 'Today's date is {{date\_time}}. This is ABSOLUTELY CRITICAL for determining if events are in the past or future.'
- Mathematical formatting and explanation style (examples):
- o 'Use LaTeX for all mathematical expressions:' (followed by example formatting)
- o 'Break down complex equations into steps rather than just presenting the final formula.'
- Visual representation guidelines (examples):
- o 'For simple concepts, use ASCII art with clear labels.'
- o 'For more complex visualizations, use SVG format.'
- Hallucinations mitigation (examples):
- o 'Distinguish between directly referenced information and logical deductions.'
- o 'NEVER fabricate answers.'
- Citations and Sources (examples):
- o 'EVERY piece of information from the context MUST have a numbered inline citation [#]'
- o 'ALWAYS append the page number if it appears after the source in the context.'

These instructions were bolstered with prompting principles from [8] including role-based and example-driven prompting, clearly stated requirements and use of delimiters (via CommonMark [9] formatting). Our Prompt Template can be seen on GitHub 11 .

## Query Topic Visualization & Analysis

Topic analysis within human-LLM conversational data, however, is a relatively new research domain with significant challenges, such as the tendency of some users not to initiate a new chat sessions when starting new conversations [11]. There is also notable asymmetry between users' typically concise, lowcontext queries (e.g. 'What is the main reason?') compared with AIs' characteristically verbose responses.

Instead of implementing a parallel pipeline to tackle this complex, multi-dimensional problem, we instead leveraged the concept of using the embedding vectors from student queries for topic analysis via clustering in embedding space. While our production system generated these in the Prompt Flow, we had not initially preserved them in the AI-TA's database. We therefore used

our text-embedding-ada-002 deployment to re-generate embeddings from the stored student queries.

First, we standardized each dimension using Z-score normalization to ensure equal contribution across all embedding dimensions. Exploratory analysis revealed this preprocessing produced more fine-grained clustering results. We believe this is because standardization prevents highvariance dimensions from dominating cluster assignment, allowing the algorithm to detect both prominent and subtle semantic patterns. ## Recommendations for AI-TA Implementers

## Positioning Custom AI-TAs Against Established Alternatives

AI-TA implementers should anticipate that their custom solution will compete directly with established AI tools for user engagement. Our survey Q6 responses provided modest evidence of this dynamic, with a few students spontaneously mentioning ChatGPT when discussing the AI-TA and drawing both positive and negative comparisons between the tools (see Table 6 for an example of the latter). This reflects ChatGPT's exceptional performance on publicly available knowledge, a phenomenon also observed by educators in other domains [3].

We recommend that AI-TA implementers focus their development efforts on scenarios where a custom tool provides clear advantages over general-purpose alternatives. Two key examples emerged in our case study:

1. Queries involving privately available information (e.g. 'when is my 3rd quiz scheduled?')
2. Queries requiring access to recent specialized knowledge before it appears in commercial training datasets. For example, while ChatGPT lacked knowledge of recent changes to FFmpeg 23 command-line syntax, our AI-TA provided accurate information since MPE course materials documented the update. This advantage proved valuable since students needed current FFmpeg syntax for assignments.

AI-TA implementers should identify similar domain-specific knowledge gaps where their solution can provide unique value that justifies user adoption alongside existing tools.

## Optimizing Deployment Costs

AI-TA implementers considering similar Azure-based solutions should carefully evaluate infrastructure costs, as they may be structured differently than anticipated. Contrary to our initial assumptions, our AI-TA's primary cost driver was not the token-based pricing of AI model usage, but rather the fixed pricing tiers of continuously running Azure services including a search engine, virtual machine, database server and a web application plan. Each service requires choosing an appropriate pricing tier based on resource needs.

Our 7-week (49-day) deployment cost €817.43, or €0.39 per student per day. Post-deployment analysis revealed that we likely over-provisioned some of these services, suggesting costs could have been reduced by approximately 40% through more careful resource allocation. We recommend AI-TA implementers carefully evaluate and right-size infrastructure services during the planning phase, as these fixed costs are incurred regardless of actual usage and may represent a significant portion of the budget. Stress testing with minimal viable configurations before production deployment may also help optimize costs.

23 https://ffmpeg.org/


## The Privacy Paradox

AI-TA implementers may need to navigate complex trade-offs between privacy protections and educational utility. We adopted usage anonymity both as an ethical safeguard to minimize personal data collection and to encourage student engagement. This decision, however, inadvertently constrained our capacity to engage students in meaningful dialogue about the AITA's effectiveness, to identify and support those grappling with specific concepts, and to cultivate collaborative conversations around system refinements. In retrospect, our approach may have been overly cautious, particularly given students' readily observable comfort with nonanonymous interactions on commercial AI platforms, where they seem to submit detailed queries without apparent privacy concerns.

However, anonymity may have been welcomed by students for different reasons, with one survey respondent expressing appreciation for having an alternative channel for asking 'loads of dumb questions' - a sentiment that proved particularly relevant given our observation of students' reticence to participate in class discussions this year. We therefore recommend that AI-TA implementers undertake a deliberate assessment of whether planned privacy measures align with both user expectations and institutional objectives, carefully weighing the potential benefits of anonymous engagement against any limitations the approach will impose on user feedback and support .

## Conclusion

This study presents a comprehensive examination of implementing a domain-specific AI Teaching Assistant (AI-TA) using Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) in a real-world educational setting. Our 7-week deployment with 43 MPE students provides practical insights into the complexities faced when deploying such systems.

## Key Findings

Our research reveals several key findings that illuminate the practical realities of AI-TA implementation in classroom settings. Assessment outcomes showed no significant exam performance differences across varying AI-TA usage levels (p-values greater than 0.05 for all pairwise comparisons), indicating that with thoughtfully designed open-book assessments, AI tools may enhance learning without compromising academic integrity.

Student feedback revealed complex attitudes toward educational AI. While 89% agreed that the AI-TA enhanced their open-book exam experience, significantly less approved of AI in that scenario when asked directly (46% of respondents that offered an opinion in an open-ended response), highlighting the value of mixed-method evaluation approaches and suggesting underlying concerns about AI's role in assessment. More generally, students viewed the AI-TA as complementing rather than replacing human tutoring.

Implementation costs at €0.39 per student per day were driven primarily by fixed Azure infrastructure costs rather than AI model usage. The lecturer's administrative workflow proved operationally intensive, requiring frequent updates and transitions between multiple tools - a significant consideration for AI-TA implementers. Providing usage anonymity may have been

appreciated by students but restricted our opportunities for feedback, targeted student support and opportunities for MPE-specific system refinement.

## Future Research

Our findings suggest that custom AI-TAs can provide value when offering clear advantages over general-purpose alternatives like ChatGPT, particularly for accessing privately available information and recent specialized knowledge.

Future development will pursue both MPE-specific enhancements and broader pedagogical refinements. The addition of multi-modal capabilities that process visual content should benefit MPE students working with visual media and illustrative diagrams. Refinement of our topic analysis implementation and methodology will lay the foundation for extension of the AI-TA to include daily recommendations for instructors based on student query patterns, enabling realtime teaching adaptation. Further workflow automation for the administrator will reduce operational burden.

This work indicates that thoughtful AI-TA deployment may enhance learning experiences while preserving academic integrity. Though implementation challenges such as user anonymity, engagement, feedback and operational efficiency require careful consideration, our experience offers practical guidance for educators and other professionals in technical fields such as MPE, who may be contemplating similar deployments.

Currently Working Parties are focusing on the following aspects:

**Terrestrial Broadcasting Delivery**

Terrestrial Broadcasting Delivery plays a vital role in providing universal, high-quality, and free-to-air delivery of audio-visual content to the public and therefore remains a crucial topic in SG 6 discussions. A key focus is the transition to second generation DTTB systems. These newer systems enhance broadcast quality and efficiency, allowing broadcasters to deliver more content and services within the same spectrum. A new second generation system, ISDB-T3, under standardization in Japan, is simultaneously under documentation in SG 6.

Additionally, developing and testing ultra-high-definition television (UHDTV) over Digital Terrestrial Television Broadcasting (DTTB) networks is a significant discussion point. These trials assess how existing infrastructures can manage the high data demands of UHDTV, which delivers superior resolution and colour quality.

New technologies like Multiple Input Multiple Output (MIMO) and Layered Division Multiplexing (LDM) techniques are under study in SG 6 with the aim to maximize spectrum efficiency, allowing broadcasters to transmit more data without compromising quality.

Moreover, the standardization of new Terrestrial Mobile Multimedia Broadcasting (TMMB) technologies designed for reaching audiences on the go, is well progressed. New trials and tests on TMMB systems, such as LTE based 5G Broadcasting and 5G New Radio, are being developed to demonstrate their capabilities and at the same time their possible challenges and ways to resolve them.

Network planning and evaluation of LTE based 5G broadcasting system has been published in a new ITU-R Report.

Complementing these technologies are efforts to expand the use of datacasting, enabling broadcasters to transmit additional data, such as weather updates, emergency alerts, or educational content, alongside traditional TV and radio broadcasts for reception by both large screen TV sets and handheld devices.

**Assembly and Access**

Working Party 6B continues to develop texts related to video & audio signal transport and multimedia, including cloud, accessibility, integrated broadcast broad band (IBB), and global platform. As content production increasingly shifts to the cloud, SG 6 is exploring how cloud-based production and transport can provide the scalability and flexibility needed for modern broadcasting.

Audio streaming formats, audio metadata, and file formats continue under active discussion. User requirements are being gathered for metadata in advanced sound systems for digital broadcasting. Ongoing work also includes aspects of audio metadata related to the Audio Definition Model of Rec. ITU-R [BS.2076](http:/www.itu.int/rec/R-REC-BS.2076/en) .

As hybrid broadcasting and broadband platforms become more prevalent, SG 6 is dedicated to ensuring their seamless integration. The Integrated Broadcast-Broadband (IBB) concept is gaining traction, enabling viewers to access both linear TV and on-demand content through a unified interface. A key example of IBB is "application-oriented television broadcasting," which seeks to merge content delivery with broadband services, transcending traditional TV channels. To support this transition, the focus must shift from middleware standardization to a comprehensive software platform specification, covering both backend infrastructure and front-end components including service navigation and viewer profile management to create a more cohesive and user-friendly system.

Trustworthiness is one of the core values of broadcasting organizations. The wide availability of simple to use, sophisticated tools based on generative-AI, has made the production of deepfakes and the manipulation of legitimate content a relatively simple process. It is becoming increasingly challenging to detect the provenance of media content. A Report is being compiled to give an overview of the work being carried out by some broadcasters and their suppliers in order to raise awareness of the development of robust systems that can be used to verify the provenance of broadcast media.

**Programme Production and Quality Assessment**

Working Party (WP) 6C studies issues and develops solutions associated with programme production and the international exchange of content for radio and television broadcasting. This also includes multimedia, interactive and converged services and quality assessment for all media.

Work on High Dynamic Range Television continues, focusing on use cases and technologies that enable single workflows for live and non-line programme production. Other HDR activates include updated test signals and the monitoring and measurement of brightness changes.

WP 6C continues to investigate accessible media services, regularly updating Report ITU-R [BT.2207](https:/www.itu.int/pub/R-REP-BT.2207) *Accessibility to broadcasting services for persons with disabilities,* adding how haptics and the use of avatars can make media more accessible to all. Energy efficient broadcasting is another key area of activity where practical advice on the requirements to report and actively reduce the impact programme production and distribution has on the environment and how this can be managed with minimal or no offsetting.

The use if AI is having a major impact on programme production and exchange of content. WP 6C is responsible for maintaining Reports ITU-R [BT.2447](https:/www.itu.int/pub/R-REP-BT.2447) on the use of AI for programme making and ITU-R BT.2524 on the future of broadcast production where examples of future workflows are presented. Work on a revision of these Reports to keep them looking forward is currently being discussed.

In other work, Report ITU-R [BT.2420](https:/www.itu.int/pub/R-REP-BT.2420) is bringing together examples of Advance Immersive Sensory Media topics which combine all aspects of programme making including volumetric image capture, advanced immersive sound, haptics and other sensory enhanced content where the merging of traditional audio and video production is creating new media experiences.

Mindful of the accelerating changes to media production, WP 6C continues to consider how subjective and objective quality assessment is carried out and measured. Recommendation ITU-R BT.500 will continue to the revised to include new techniques (AI and ML QC) and new environments (immersive AV).

WP 6C collaborates with WP 6B on topics related to content provenance, immersive sound systems (ADM and SADM), cloud processing and with WP 6A on how new content types can be delivered through new distribution systems.

**Conclusion**

During its current 2024-2027 study cycle, SG 6 is continuing to push the boundaries of broadcasting technology, ensuring that broadcasters remain at the forefront of innovation. Artificial intelligence (AI) is expected to become increasingly important, with AI-driven content curation set to transform viewer engagement by delivering personalized content based on user preferences and viewing habits.

SG 6 will continue its collaboration with industry partners, including organizations such as SMPTE and other ITU Study Groups, harmonizing standards and fostering interoperability across platforms and regions. This collaboration is key to ensuring that broadcasting technologies evolve in a way that benefits the global community, maintaining broadcasting’s role as a vital public service.

<1-hop>


**Consumer Technology Association**

**Brian Markwalter**

2025 is a year of change in the TV business.  Streaming is now consumers’ top choice for watching TV, by preferred video source, time spent viewing, and other common measures.  According to Pew Research Center, 83% of Americans watch streaming services, and for 55% of Americans streaming is their only source.  28% of Americans “double dip,” both subscribing to cable or satellite and watching streaming services.  Time spent viewing these sources followed suit. This year Nielsen reported, “Streaming reached a historic milestone in May as its share of total television usage outpaced the combined share of broadcast and cable for the first time ever.”

What about antenna usage? It is a distant third.  In Pew’s study, antenna users land in the “neither subscribe to cable or satellite nor watch streaming services” group, representing just 8% of consumers.  Another way to look at antenna usage is how many homes can access live TV via an antenna.  Horowitz Research says this figure declined from 32% in 2020 to 19% in 2025.  Nielsen’s public data is a little older, from January 2024, but matches Horowitz. Nielsen said that 22.75 million US households, or 18% of the 125 million TV households, access content through an antenna.

What has not changed is that Americans love their screens – and movies and TV shows. Televisions and smartphones are the top two technology products in U.S. consumers’ homes by a wide margin, with near-total penetration at 95% each. Laptops complete the screen trifecta with 73% ownership. According to CTA’s *The Video Ecosystem: The Future of TV report* , 85% of Americans reported watching movies and 82% reported watching TV shows in the past three months. News is third at 58%, and the combination of live sports, music videos, and long- and short-forum user generated content are all middle of the pack with about 50%.


The CTA Technology and Standards team has been busy working with industry to ensure consumers’ video entertainment experience gets better every year.  Here are some areas where our work made the biggest impact.

HDMI and CTA-861

Since its first publication in 2001, CTA-861 ( *A DTV Profile for Uncompressed High Speed Digital Interfaces* ) has played a critical role in the transition from analog to digital video interfaces on TVs and a wide range of other displays and video sources.  CTA-861 has a particularly symbiotic relationship with HDMI, underpinning audio and video signaling between sources and displays that use HDMI.  As A/V technology improves, CTA-861 needs regular updates to keep up with the needs of industry.  The standards committee that maintains CTA-861 has settled into a rhythm, producing a new baseline standard every two to three years.  Each major revision gets a new version letter following the standard number. The latest and greatest CTA-861 is revision J.  Changes in CTA-861-J include the following:

- Combined CTA-861-I with improvements contained in CTA-861.7
- Aligned Speaker Allocation Data Block (SADB) with industry requirements
- Added support for new features of VESA CVT in Video Timing Data Blocks (VTDBs)
- Clarified Data Blocks and InfoFrames, including defaultRGB, in the Colorimetry Data Block
- Deprecated DRA audio
- And as always, updated references

It’s not all about paperwork and PDFs.  CTA also hosts an annual CTA-861 Plugfest event.  CTA’s 861 Plugfest, typically held each October in California, brings manufacturers together to test interfaces, such as HDMI, HDCP and CEC, as part of a semi-private, round robin event.

The WAVE Project

The CTA WAVE Project (Web Application Video Ecosystem Project), which works to improve the global interoperability of internet-delivered commercial video, celebrated its 10 th anniversary in 2025. The WAVE Project references accepted industry standards like HTML5, MSE/EME, CENC, DASH, and HLS. As a key aspect of the project, participants maintain a complete, normative streaming player environment specification and interoperability tests to enable broad deployment of internet-delivered streaming media services. WAVE also enhances content delivery efficiencies and quality of service, with new protocols to exchange performance and route tracing data between clients and upstream sources such as Content Delivery Networks. The project also hosts the CMAF Industry Forum (CMAF-IF), which promotes CMAF industry interoperability and support.

WAVE has work underway on content preparation, web media API device support, device playback quality and validation, and standardized performance metadata exchanged between media clients and servers. Some specifications are paired with free open-source test programs and content to verify content and device performance. For example, the WAVE team has improved the device test suite released last year to make it easier to install and added new features, such as support for HEVC.

WAVE maintains key industry specifications, including the *Content Specification* (CTA-5001-F), an annual update to the *Web Media API Snapshot* (CTA-5000-H), *Device Playback Capabilities Specification* (CTA-5003-B), and *DASH-HLS Interoperability Specification* (CTA-5005-B). WAVE is also working on specifications to improve the flow of media to devices, including the *Common Media Client Data Specification* (CTA-5004-A), *Common Media Server Data* (CTA-5006), *Common Access Token Specification* (CTA-5007-B), and *Request Tracing Specification* (CTA-5008). WAVE also standardized the popular GeoHash specification as *Fast and Readable Geographical Hashing* (CTA-5009-A).

WAVE has also released an updated version of the *WAVE Streaming Media Test Suite for Devices* , a free open-source smart TV/media stick/set-top-box test suite for performance and compatibility verification of client platforms.

Energy Efficiency

Under two voluntary industry programs developed by CTA and NCTA, leading internet, cable, satellite, and telco service providers and equipment manufacturers continue to drive energy efficiency gains for set-top boxes, broadband modems, routers, and gateways. Leading TV manufacturers are making similar strides under a CTA-developed program.

Set-top box annual energy consumption fell by nearly three-quarters since 2012. A significant portion of this decline is due to subscriber reductions, but the weighted average power consumption of new set-top boxes also decreased by nearly two-thirds since 2013, even as functionality and features increased. This program uses ANSI/CTA-2043-B, Set-top Box (STB) Power Measurement.

Modems, routers and gateways all saw dramatic drops in the energy it takes to provide a gigabit of bandwidth to the consumer. Power per bit has been reduced by well over 80% and in some cases close to 90% since 2015. This program uses ANSI/CTA-2049-B, Determination of Small Network Equipment Average Energy Consumption, which will be incorporated into a new IEC standard (IEC 62087-8) to facilitate international harmonization.

Leading TV makers agreed to a standby power limit of 2 watts, a threshold that will go into effect in 2026. Negotiations toward an on-mode limit continue. The TV voluntary agreement is based on ANSI/CTA-2037-D, Determination of Television Set Power Consumption, now the U.S. Department of Energy test procedure for TVs. This agreement will also be incorporated into an IEC standard (IEC 62087-3) to facilitate international harmonization.

NEXTGEN TV


ATSC 3.0 is made possible by the transmission standards created by ATSC, but the toolbox of capabilities in ATSC 3.0 exceeds what any practical TV receiver can support. CTA fulfills a unique role in the ecosystem by producing the CTA-CEB32 suite of recommended practices for ATSC 3.0 TVs – closing the loop between transmission standards and receivers. CTA-CEB32 is a 10-part set of documents written for industry as guidance when designing ATSC 3.0 TVs.  CTA also developed the NEXTGEN TV logo program, so that consumers can easily identify ATSC 3.0 compatible TVs. Products bearing the NEXTGEN TV logo must pass an extensive suite of interoperability tests before going to market.  Every year the NEXTGEN TV test suite is updated to add tests as industry identifies new ATSC 3.0 features and interoperability concerns. The 2025 test suite now includes 475 tests and adds support for HDR10 playback and updated API schemas for interactivity support.

## The State of Sustainability in the Media Technology Industry, 2025

*SMPTE Progress Report 2025*

*By Barbara Lange, Founder and CEO at Kibo121*

The media technology sector stands at a critical inflection point. As video now accounts for more than 80% of global internet traffic, the energy and carbon impacts of media creation, distribution, and consumption are very real. The industry has made progress.  Green production standards are widely adopted, awareness is growing, and voluntary initiatives have gained traction, but systemic challenges remain. Reports from leading industry bodies reveal a picture of cautious progress: sustainability is rising in importance, but often still takes a back seat to cost and efficiency. Against this backdrop, the Media Tech Sustainability Series (MTSS) launched the Media Climate Accord (MCA) at IBC 2025, a framework designed to unify efforts and accelerate measurable progress across the global media ecosystem.

### Green Productions Lead the Way: EBU’s Practical Work

Production environments have seen the most visible advances. The European Broadcasting Union (EBU) has published in-depth reports on the green practices of the International Biathlon Union, offering actionable toolkits for broadcasters to reduce environmental impact. These [best practices](https:/tech.ebu.ch/groups/greenproduction) serve as guiding tools for members.

EBU has also been profiling the energy consumption of generators on sets, providing producers with data to make informed choices about greener alternatives. The organization is equally focused on storytelling, exploring how broadcasters take their staff on the sustainability journey and embed climate messaging into audience-facing content. Finally, EBU is contributing to [IBC’s Accelerator project, EcoFlow II](https:/show.ibc.org/accelerator-project-ecoflow-ii) , on measuring streaming distribution, where early models are providing insight into the environmental costs of different delivery paths.

### Streaming and Distribution: Greening of Streaming’s Evidence Base

Distribution remains a blind spot, but the [Greening of Streaming](https:/www.greeningofstreaming.org) consortium has been filling the gaps. Over the past 18 months, its hackathon series has become the backbone of experimentation. What began with smart plug tests now spans router monitoring, peer-to-peer delivery trials, compression experiments, and videoconferencing comparisons. Findings are sometimes counterintuitive: for example, HD playback on certain 4K TVs consumes 3–5% *more* energy than native 4K. Peer-to-peer delivery tests showed content could reach six clients with just 0.1W of additional power for the active node.

The group’s technical work is also breaking new ground. Its E-YANG protocol, a real-time [YANG-based method](https:/en.wikipedia.org/wiki/YANG) for reporting power data, is now with the [IETF](https:/www.ietf.org) for standardization. Meanwhile, the real-time energy measurement work enables granular measurement of device energy usage. Beyond technology, Greening of Streaming emphasizes community to share recommendations while building a shared evidence-based knowledge.

### Standards and Measurement: ATSC and SMPTE

Standards bodies are increasingly embedding sustainability into their technical work. The Advanced Television Systems Committee (ATSC) created [Planning Team 9](https:/www.atsc.org/subcommittees/planning-team-9-sustainability) (PT9) in 2023 to study how broadcast data delivery can contribute to energy-efficient media.

PT9 has built a rich knowledge base through tutorials and expert input, covering a variety of relevant topics.  Its current tasks are concrete: developing methods to measure energy consumption of delivery methods, tracking organizational progress toward sustainability, collaborating with peer organizations, and identifying potential standards or recommended practices to embed sustainability into the technical fabric of broadcasting.

[SMPTE](https:/www-smpte-org.sandbox.hs-sites.com/projects?__hstc=52635383.f871bb2fb2553d6ccbbb0df5a5bfb417.1758136465014.1758136465014.1758136465014.1&__hssc=52635383.1.1758136465014&__hsfp=1811316718) has established a dedicated Study Group on Sustainability to examine how standards development can support climate goals. The group is exploring requirements and use cases where embedding sustainability into technical specifications could drive measurable impact. Its internal report, expected by late 2025, will provide guidance on priority areas for standards activity and opportunities for collaboration with other bodies such as ATSC, EBU, and ITU.

### Market Trends and Surveys: Mixed Signals

Several recent surveys shed light on industry attitudes toward sustainability.

- [IABM](https:/theiabm.org) Industry Tracker: Sustainability is rising in importance but remains secondary to total cost of ownership and efficiency. AI adoption is a double-edged sword, it boosts efficiency but increases energy demands, driving awareness of sustainability as a counterbalance. European buyers are leading the way, with RFPs often including mandatory sustainability criteria.
- [Broadcast Tech Survey 2025](https:/www.broadcastnow.co.uk/tech/get-early-access-to-the-big-broadcast-tech-survey-2025/5206071.article) : Only 30% of respondents said sustainability is central to purchasing decisions. Still, 82% are investing in tools to measure and reduce impact, and nearly half see sustainability as at least a medium priority. The survey highlights uneven cloud adoption and patchy integration of AI, with cost cited as the main barrier.
- [Devoncroft Big Broadcast Survey](https:/devoncroft.com/2025/08/04/2025-big-broadcast-survey-bbs-reports-now-available) : In global rankings, sustainability placed 20th out of 22 industry trends. Strikingly, 70% of vendors said sustainability has no impact on customers’ sourcing decisions. Yet regional variation is strong: Western European buyers value sustainability nearly four times more than their North American peers.
- [DPP Sustainability Pulse Check](https:/www.thedpp.com/news/sustainability-pulse-check-2025-reveals-industry-attitudes-to-green-agenda) : Offering a more optimistic view, the DPP found that half of organizations see sustainability as a high priority, and two-thirds expect it to grow in importance in the next 1–3 years. Again, the split is geographic—European broadcasters show higher commitment, while many US vendors still treat sustainability as peripheral.

Together, these surveys show progress but underline fragmentation. For many companies, sustainability is acknowledged but not decisive in business strategy.

### MTSS and the Media Climate Accord: A Framework for Alignment

Since its inception, the [Media Tech Sustainability Series](https:/www.mtsseries.org) (MTSS) has convened the global media ecosystem to elevate sustainability as a leadership issue through its activities including sharing of best practices, webinars, the annual Summit, and content presented at industry events.  At IBC 2025, MTSS convened the first show floor tour of vendors focused on sustainability efforts.

Also at IBC 2025, MTSS launched the [Media Climate Accord](https:/www.mtsseries.org/media-climate-accord) (MCA), which aims to unite broadcasters, streamers, content creators, and technology vendors around a shared commitment to reach net-zero emissions by 2040-2050. It provides a structured but voluntary framework for signatories to measure, report, and take action to reduce emissions across the entire value chain, from production and post to distribution and consumption.

The Accord promotes best-practice sharing, industry engagement, and collaborative innovation. By aligning fragmented initiatives into one cohesive framework, the MCA positions the media industry as a credible, proactive player in addressing the climate crisis.

The vision for a sustainable ecosystem by 2040 is ambitious but clear: infrastructure powered by renewables, modular and circular hardware, efficient distribution, transparent supply chains, and informed audiences. The MCA is positioned as the vehicle to make this vision achievable.

Barbara Lange, from [Kibo121](https:/www.kibo121.io) , highlights the unevenness across the media value chain. Production has made significant strides, but sustainability efforts often lose momentum once content enters the “digital factory” of post-production, archiving, and mastering. Distribution, too, suffers from a lack of standardized, real-world measurement of energy use and emissions.  Thankfully, industry groups are tackling these areas.

And still, vendors are increasingly asked for sustainability credentials in RFPs, and broadcasters are rewarding partners who share their efforts.  This process helps push the sustainability agenda.

### Conclusion: From Fragmentation to Alignment

The state of sustainability in media technology today is one of cautious progress, persistent fragmentation, and emerging alignment. Surveys show sustainability is not yet a top commercial driver, but its importance is growing, particularly in Europe and among larger organizations. Industry bodies are increasingly engaged with better understanding the true energy costs across the media ecosystem.

The launch of the Media Climate Accord represents a watershed moment. For the first time, the industry has a unifying structure to measure, compare, and accelerate action across the value chain. Adoption will require collective will, but if embraced, the MCA could shift sustainability from a peripheral concern to a central driver of innovation, investment, and leadership in the media technology industry.

## Data is Not a Byproduct-It's the Product:

## Applying Data-as-a-Product Thinking in Media & Entertainment

## Dan Gesshel, Founder & Principal, Elevate Digital Strategy

## Written for presentation at the

## SMPTE 2025 Media and Technology Summit

## Abstract .

The Media & Entertainment industry is generating more data than ever before, yet much of his data is underutilized. Decades of centralized architectures, fragmented and siloed ownership, and tooldriven initiatives have produced data lakes and dashboards, but not trusted, scalable insights the industry needs. At the same time, the rise of artificial intelligence has made the availability of high quality, accessible data more critical than ever.

This paper argues for a shift to a Data as a Product (DaaP), supported by the architectural framework of a Data Mesh, as a path to unlocking value, and securing the necessary trust. By treating data with the same discipline as software products, complete with ownership, lifecycle management, service-level agreements (SLAs), and feedback loops, organizations can establish trust, reusability, and accountability. The paper outlines the three planes of a Data Mesh (infrastructure utility, mesh experience, and data product experience), defines what constitutes a true data product within this model, and highlights rights management as a representative use case where productization resolves longstanding pain points.

Finally, the paper examines barriers to adoption and offers a roadmap to success. Benefits include faster insights, reduced costs, new monetization opportunities, AI readiness, and productivity gains. For Media & Entertainment companies facing rising complexity and competition, Data as a Product is no longer optional. It is a business imperative.

Keywords. Data as a Product, DaaP, Data Mesh, Media and Entertainment, Content Supply Chain, Data Architecture, Data Governance, Data Pipelines, Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning.

## Introduction

There has been an explosion of data in society. The cost of storage has fallen dramatically, making it easier than ever to capture and warehouse information. At the same time, the rise of artificial intelligence has made the availability of high-quality data critical for better, faster, and more meaningful decisions. Nowhere is this more evident than in Media & Entertainment, where the pace at which data is both created and consumed is frenetic. Audience behavior, rights production, and localization all intersect, making data central to every creative, operational, and business decision [8].

Yet the industry faces two major challenges. First, while much attention has been given to AI and machine learning, there is less recognition that these capabilities are entirely dependent on the quality and accessibility of the underlying data. Second, despite substantial investments, often in the millions of dollars, in tools, warehouses, and data lakes, most organizations still struggle to leverage their data effectively.

This paper argues that treating data as a product, complete with ownership, lifecycles, and service-level agreements, provides a path to unlock scalable value. We will first examine why traditional approaches have fallen short, then define what it means to 'productize' data and outline the principles of product thinking. From there, we explore the architecture and processes behind a Data Mesh platform, and conclude with strategies for execution and adoption, two areas often overlooked but critical to success.

## Why Current Approaches Fall Short

The current approaches to data have consistently fallen short of their promised utopia of fully democratized, easily accessible data and a single source of truth. For years, organizations have been told that success would come through toolsets, dashboards, and pipelines. Budgets grew, teams expanded, yet the results remain disappointing. Trust in data continues to lag, with questions about accuracy, reliability, and usefulness persisting across the enterprise [6].

The gap between what was promised and what was delivered is stark, as shown in Figure 1 , which contrasts 'What We Were Told' versus 'What We Actually Got.' The single source of truth has often devolved into, 'which version is this?' Dashboards meant to empower users instead leave executives calling analysts to pull reports manually. Centralization was supposed to reduce fragmentation, but too often it resulted in data no one knew how to use. Even realtime pipelines, heralded as the solution to latency, still left analysts telling stakeholders they would have to wait weeks for reporting. The idea of 'build once, use everywhere' instead became 'copied five times into different tools.'

Figure 1. What We Were Told vs. What We Got


To be fair, progress has been made. Centralized data lakes, ETL tools, and BI platforms have improved access and standardization in many areas, but most organizations remain stuck in the same loop. Data is not trusted, no one truly owns it, and reuse is minimal. Bottlenecks persist as requests queue up with data engineering teams, reinforcing gatekeeping rather than selfservice.

The impacts are not abstract. In Media & Entertainment, fragile approaches to data create real operational risks. Global rights and localization workflows break down, distribution metadata mismatches disrupt partner ingestion, and reporting delays slow decision-making in production and marketing. What has been built is infrastructure, but without the ability to fully leverage it.

If data is to be treated as a true business asset, and scaled for AI and other advanced use cases, it cannot remain a byproduct of pipelines and tooling. It must be managed as a product: owned, supported, and designed for use.

## Defining Data as a Product

Before we go further, it is important to outline the principles of product thinking. In Media & Entertainment, a 'product' usually means content such as a film, a series, or a brand. In technology, however, a product is something designed, built and supported to solve a user's problem over time. It has a clear purpose, defined users, ownership, and a lifecycle that includes roadmaps, metrics, and continuous improvement. Treating data like a product means managing it intentionally, ensuring it is discoverable, usable, and accountable, just as one would for a digital application or streaming platform.

Data as a Product (DaaP) is not a new idea, but the stakes have changed. For years, organizations centralized their data into lakes and warehouses, assuming a single repository would unlock value. In practice, this model created bottlenecks and brittle pipelines. Data Mesh,

a concept introduced in 2015, proposed a federated model where domains own their data products, but operate on a shared platform with governance and standards [1]. Still, adoption lagged. The rise of generative AI in 2023 changed the equation. Speed and accessibility became paramount, and traditional infrastructure could no longer keep up. What was once an interesting idea has become a strategic imperative.

This raises the question of what actually makes something a data product? For many years, access has been ad hoc. JIRA tickets with weeks-long SLAs, CSV dumps emailed around, or dashboards that answered a question once, but quickly went stale. None of these are data products. They are brittle outputs, not reusable assets. This distinction is illustrated in Figure 2 , which contrasts common outputs such as dashboards and file dumps with the characteristics of a true data product.

Figure 2. Not a Data Product vs. Data Product


A true data product is designed, maintained, and supported to solve a recurring problem for a defined user or domain. It has a clear use case, an interface, and ownership. It is documented, discoverable, and versioned, with service-level agreements (SLAs) and observability metrics. While its internals may involve complex joins, pipelines, and validation, the user experience is clean and reliable, an API or UI they can trust. This abstraction expands the audience far beyond engineers to analysts, developers, partners, and business leaders, who can all consume and reuse it with confidence. In short, a data product transforms messy, technical data into something accessible, scalable, and trustworthy. The components of a data product are summarized in Figure 3 , which shows how inputs, transformations, outputs, and discoverability features come together in a single, reusable unit. This visualization is adapted from the framework introduced by Zhamak Dehghani in Data Mesh (2021) [6].

Figure 3. Anatomy of a Data Product


## Architecture and Process

## Refinery to Pumps Analogy

To understand the shift in data architecture, consider the analogy of oil. Organizations need oil to fuel different kinds of vehicles, just as they need data to fuel business initiatives, dashboards, ad hoc requests, or AI models. However, each vehicle requires a specific type of fuel, and the oil must be refined before it can be used.

In the traditional model, all the oil (data) is sent to a single refinery, the centralized data warehouse or lake. When a request comes in, the refinery produces the right fuel, but with one pump operated by a data engineer, everyone waits. Fine at small scale, but it breaks at enterprise demand.

The alternative is many smaller refineries, each specialized in a particular kind of fuel. These refineries, domain-owned data products, know everything about their data, including its lineage and quality. They provide it through dedicated pumps (APIs) that users can access directly, without an attendant. All of these refineries sit on a unified platform, a Data Mesh that ensures compliance and shared standards eliminating bottlenecks and enabling self-service at scale. This transition is illustrated in Figure 4 , which contrasts the centralized refinery model with a mesh of self-serve pumps representing domain-owned data products.

Figure 4. From One Refinery to Self-Serve Pumps


This analogy illustrates the benefits of shifting to a Data as a Product model. In a Data Mesh, products sit on a shared platform that provides standards for authentication, SLAs, and observability, while exposing outputs through self-service APIs. Each product is owned by its domain experts, who are accountable for quality and lineage, building trust across the enterprise. Governance is applied automatically through policies and automation, rather than central gatekeeping. The result is data that is both accessible and reliable, with complexity abstracted away so users across the organization can focus on outcomes rather than infrastructure.

## Lessons from Software Architecture

The evolution of data architecture mirrors the evolution of software. Early applications were monoliths: tightly coupled code where one fault could crash the whole system, the infamous Windows 'blue screen of death.' .

Software engineering solved this challenge by shifting to microservices. Instead of one giant, interdependent codebase, systems were broken into smaller, domain-specific services, each with its own interface, lifecycle and accountability. Teams with expertise in a specific area could build, maintain, and evolve their service independently. The result was improved scalability, resilience, and the ability to continuously deliver improvements without breaking the entire application. This mirrors the broader shift in platform thinking described by Parker et al. in Platform Revolution [2].

Data is now making the same transition. Centralized data lakes and brittle pipelines resemble the monoliths of early software. They are giving way to domain-owned data products, designed like microservices that are autonomous, accountable, and interoperable within a larger Data

Mesh. This shift enables the same benefits of greater resilience, scalability, and innovation. This evolution is shown in Figure 5, which compares the shift from monolithic software to microservices with the ongoing transition from centralized data lakes to domain-owned data products.

Figure 5. Software Evolved. Data Didn't. Until Now


The Data Mesh platform is the foundation for moving to this new style of architecture and process. It is where all of your data products sit and function from, and provides a unified user experience across all of your data. It's where governance and standardization is applied, as well as global policy enforcement, monitoring, and a host of other aspects that enable the level of control that's needed. There are three areas we'll discuss briefly that are used across a Data Mesh: the Infrastructure Utility Plane, the Mesh Experience Plane, and the Data Product Experience Plane. This model builds on the framework introduced by Zhamak Dehghani in Data Mesh (2021) [1] and is summarized in Figure 6 .

Figure 6. The Three Planes of a Data Mesh


Think of your Infrastructure Utility Plane like your plumbing, and how you scale, your Mesh Experience Plane how you discover and govern, and your Data Product Experience Plane how you take ownership of the data.

## The Three Planes of a Data Mesh

## Infrastructure Utility Plane

The Infrastructure Utility Plane is the plumbing of the Data Mesh, the shared foundation that every data product depends on. It abstracts away complexity so that individual domains don't need to reinvent infrastructure, while enforcing consistency in scale, reliability, and costefficiency across the enterprise.

Core components include storage and warehouses (S3, Azure Data Lake, Snowflake), compute (Spark, Flink, serverless options such as AWS Lambda), and orchestration (Airflow, dbt). It supports observability and monitoring (Prometheus, Datadog), security (IAM, OAuth), and

CI/CD (Jenkins, GitHub Actions). Most organizations already have these. The mesh standardizes their use across domains.

By providing guardrails without gatekeeping, the Infrastructure Utility Plane ensures that domains can innovate without sacrificing consistency. It offers a common technical foundation that all data products share, making them easier to scale, manage, and trust without constraining domain autonomy.

## Mesh Experience Plane

The Mesh Experience Plane provides the user-facing layer for finding, understanding, and trusting data products. It ensures that governance and compliance are applied automatically, rather than through manual oversight, making the mesh discoverable, observable, and interoperable across the enterprise.

Core capabilities include discovery and cataloging (Collibra, Alation), lineage and metadata (Apache Atlas, OpenLineage), and observability and monitoring (Monte Carlo, OpenTelemetry). Policy enforcement is also embedded at this level, handing access controls, privacy rules such as GDPR and CCPA, and usage policies through platforms like Immuta. Finally, this plane supports search and query interfaces such as APIs or catalog-driven browsing. In practice, pairing catalog-driven discovery with governed self-service data preparation reduces ticket queues and accelerates time-to-insight [5].

The key is that every data product becomes self-describing with documentation, lineage, contracts, and SLOs visible to users. Policies are enforced automatically at the mesh level, reducing bottlenecks and ensuring consistency across domains. The result is a trusted ecosystem where users know who owns a product, what 'good' looks like, and whether they can rely on it.

## Data Product Experience Plane

The Data Product Experience Plane is where data products come to life for users and applications. It provides the interfaces, documentation, and contracts that make products consumable, reliable, and available for self-service. This is the layer where data products meet their consumers.

Core components include APIs and streaming outputs (REST, GraphQL, Kafka), documentation and schema contracts (OpenAPI, AsyncAPI), and versioning and lifecycle management (Gitbased workflows, semantic versioning). To ensure a consistent experience across the enterprise, products may also expose standardized UI portals or SDKs for access. Quality is supported by testing and validation frameworks such as dbt tests or Great Expectations. Each product includes clear ownership metadata, SLOs, and usage metrics.

The value of this plane is consistency and accessibility. Products are consumable through standard interfaces, supported by their domains, and backed by contracts and metrics that users can trust. By abstracting away infrastructure and complexity, the Data Product Experience Plane enables analysts, developers, partners, and business leaders to repeatedly leverage data at a scale.

Taken together, the three planes of the Data Mesh form a complete system for making data consumable, scalable, and trusted across the enterprise. The Infrastructure Utility Plane provides the technical foundation, storage, compute, pipelines and deployment, without forcing every domain to reinvent complexity. The Mesh Experience Plane ensures that products are discoverable, observable, and governed through automation, making interoperability and trust built-in from the start rather than bolted on later. Finally, the Data Product Experience Plane connects products to their consumers through APIs, documentation, contracts, and clear ownership, ensuring consistency and reliability.

It is the integration of these planes that allows the Data Mesh to scale effectively. Infrastructure without experience is invisible, experience without governance is untrustworthy, and data products without consistency are unusable.

## Data Products Inside The Mesh

The Data Mesh only delivers value when domains build and maintain their own products. A data product delivers information that is consumable, reliable, and reusable, with clear accountability and lifecycle management. Its inputs may include upstream APIs, event streams, or batch sources. It contains the transformation and business logic needed for modeling, validation, and enrichment (often implemented in tools like dbt or Spark). Its outputs are defined in advance by the product owner and exposed through APIs, feeds, or exports. In addition, every product publishes a discoverability API, a self-describing contract with schemas, lineage, ownership, documentation, observability metrics, and sample data. Products are versioned, change managed, and explicitly tied to a domain team and owner for full transparency. An example technical view of a data product is shown in Figure 7 , which builds on the framework introduced by Zhamak Dehghani in Data Mesh (2021) [1], highlighting its inputs, transformations, outputs, and discoverability interfaces.

Figure 7. Technical View of a Data Product


Domain teams have full autonomy over how their products are built and evolved, and not the centralized data team. They are accountable for its reliability, quality, and compliance using the various planes and standards on the data mesh. This ensures a balance that the data products are both domain specific and interoperable across the enterprise. In practice, this means every data product behaves like a miniature software service. It has contracts, interfaces, metrics, and an owner. This makes it usable and trustworthy, not just by its home domain, but across the entire enterprise.

## Use Case: Rights Tracker API

Now that we have established what a Data Mesh and what a data product consists of, we can turn to a practical example that illustrates its impact. Rights management is one of the most critical and complex domains in Media & Entertainment, and it provides a clear case study for how Data as a Product resolves longstanding challenges.

A Rights Tracker API reframes the challenge as a data product, instead of siloed spreadsheets and one-off reports. The Rights Domain publishes an API that can be queried in real-time by internal teams with clear, contract-driven responses to common business questions (e.g. Is this title licensed for Germany next month? Which platforms can show this series in Latin America today? When does the distribution window expire in North America?) As shown in Figure 8 , fragmented rights data from multiple sources is synthesized into a governed Rights Tracker API that provides clear outputs for legal, distribution, and marketing teams.

Figure 8. Rights Tracker API as a Data Product


The Rights Domain team maintains the logic that translates the legal contracts into machinereadable rules based on user requirements and feedback. They are fully accountable for the data product and its outputs, while ensuring compliance with enterprise governance standards. Observability provides metrics on freshness and reliability, giving downstream users confidence. Discoverability means that legal, distribution, and marketing teams can all access the same rights data product without building redundant processes.

By productizing rights as an API, Media & Entertainment organizations gain efficiency in managing information across domains. Scheduling, localization, and distribution can all integrate a trusted foundational element into their workflows with confidence. In an industry where compliance is non-negotiable, and errors are costly, the Rights Tracker API shows how treating data as a product transforms a fragile domain into a reusable enterprise asset. While this paper focused on rights management, the same principles apply to other domains such as localization, partner metadata packages, and audience segmentation APIs, each benefiting from clear ownership, contracts, and discoverability.

Rights and distribution metadata practices are not invented in isolation. Media & Entertainment workflows already rely on a set of SMPTE standards that address interoperability and metadata consistency across domains, including ST 2067 (Interoperable Master Format, ST 2125 (Mapping MXF to AXF), and ST 2102 (Core Metadata Set). Referencing and aligning with these

standards ensures that new data products, such as Rights Tracker API, can integrate cleanly with established industry practices while providing the flexibility of a productized, self-serve model.

## Barriers to Adoption

The question then becomes what's stopping organizations from doing this, and why even with clear product principles (Data as a Product) and technical architecture (Data Mesh,) organizations often struggle to move forward. The four most common areas that usually cause this are lack of ownership, poor trust in the data and process, organizational silos, and overreliance on technology alone. Lack of explicit ownership leaves data adrift without accountability. Poor trust in data erodes confidence before new product can even gain traction. Siloed structures cause gatekeeping and prevent collaboration across domains. Many companies simply believe throwing more tools and a larger budget will solve the problem. Industry research confirms that organizations consistently underestimate the scale of governance and adoption challenges, leaving many initiatives stalled before they can deliver business value [6]. These systemic issues also explain why so many data initiatives fail to deliver on their value, even if the underlying technology is sound. They create conditions in which two 'silent killers' emerge repeatedly: poor execution and lack of go-to-market.

## Poor Execution

Poor execution is one of the most consistent reasons Data as a Product, (or any product), fails to deliver. Execution is not adoption. It's whether the product is built, delivered, and supported to the required standard with proper leadership and sponsorship. This isn't about assigning it to a project manager or ad hoc team. It requires disciplined, cross-functional execution to define outcomes, roadmaps, and metrics. Partnerships across engineering, UX, QA, and operations prevent gaps or misalignment. SLAs/SLOs, ownership of quality, backlogs, and accountability must be established. Execution also requires listening to customers, both internal and external, about their needs. Strong execution demands leadership that understands the difference between shipping a dataset and delivering a product. Without this foundation, even the bestdesigned strategies or architectures cannot succeed.

## No Go-To-Market

The second silent killer is the oversight, or absence, of a go-to-market strategy. Many assume this is the job of training or marketing or believe a product will succeed simply because it is needed. This is not the case. Even with strong execution, a data product will fail if no one knows it exists, understands its value, or trusts it enough to adopt. Go-to-market is not about selling, but about intentional strategies to drive awareness and sustained use. Too often, data teams assume 'if you build it, they will come,' only to see users revert to legacy tools. Lack of onboarding, documentation, advocacy, and feedback loops are hallmarks of a weak strategy.

You must ensure adoption of the data product is not left to chance. Treat internal users like customers requiring education, communication, and advocacy. Have clear onboarding paths, engage champions across the enterprise, proper documentation and materials, and evidence through metrics and case studies. Have a feedback mechanism and listen to your customers to evolve the data product as you go. This is the path to success. Without a deliberate go-to-

market plan, even the best built data products will fail to deliver on their potential because users will never make them part of their daily workflows.

## Adoption Roadmap and Operating Model

## Adoption Roadmap

Adoption of data products isn't instantaneous and needs to be staged for success. A phased approach enables progress without trying to boil the ocean. Start with a pilot. Expand with 2 - 3 additional products showing clear ROI, adding, 'just enough' standards and reusable components to form a lightweight Data Mesh platform. Then scale: enable self-service with catalog, CI/CD, and observability. Bring in SLAs/SLOs and governance, not for gatekeeping, but for broad domain ownership. This paper has argued that the shift to Data as a Product, supported by the architecture and governance of a Data Mesh, provides a path forward. Treating data with the same discipline as software establishes ownership, accountability, and most importantly trust. The three planes of the mesh create a foundation for infrastructure, governance, and consumption, while data products deliver value as autonomous, reusable units.
